content.text:
The courtyard repair bench stood beneath a fig tree, with jars of nails lined up along its back. Beside it sat the shared toy cart, blue as a summer sky and scratched from years of hauling dolls, books, and flowerpots. Its left front wheel gave a sharp little rattle whenever anyone pushed it.

Ada wanted to fix the cart before the rain came. More than that, she wanted Mr. Rafi to trust her with the tools at the bench. Niko had six young tomato plants waiting in a tray, and the roof’s downspout spilled water right where they stood.

“Can I borrow your small spanner?” Ada asked Mr. Rafi. “The cart’s left wheel is loose.”

Mr. Rafi handed her the spanner. “Is it loose, or does it rattle?”

Ada glanced at the wheel. “It rattles.”

“That’s a sound,” he said, smiling. “Bring the cart over here and have a look.”

But Niko was already carrying the tray of plants toward the courtyard gate. The clouds above the rooftops were dark and swollen. Ada wheeled the cart to the bench and crouched beside the noisy wheel. It looked much like the others. She gave its nut a turn with the spanner, then another. The wheel stopped rattling.

“There,” she said.

She spun it to check. It barely moved. Ada frowned and tightened the nut once more, thinking the wheel must have been crooked.

Niko set the tray in the cart. “Ready?”

Ada pushed. The cart lurched forward, then stopped with a scrape. The left wheel had locked.

“We can drag it,” Niko said. “The plants need to get away from the drain.”

Ada looked at the heavy tray, then at the wheel. If they dragged it, the cart might tip, or the wheel might break. She could pretend the scrape was nothing. Instead, she gripped the cart’s handle.

“Wait. I made it worse,” she said. “Let’s put the plants under the bench while I figure it out.”

Niko’s mouth tightened, but he helped her lift the tray down. The first raindrops spotted the paving stones.

Ada carried the spanner back to Mr. Rafi. “The nut wasn’t loose,” she said. “I tightened it, and now the wheel won’t turn.”

“All right,” he said. “What can you check before turning it again?”

Ada thought. Then she tipped the cart carefully onto its side. She held the wheel still and rocked the cart. No rattle. She spun the wheel. A dry click came once with every turn.

“Something’s inside,” she said.

Mr. Rafi steadied the cart while Ada loosened the nut. She slid off the wheel and found a tight green loop of kite string pinched between the hub and the washer. One frayed end tapped the inside of the wheel each time it turned. The nut had been snug all along; the string had made the wheel clatter and drag.

Niko peered over her shoulder. “That’s from my kite. I thought the tail had come loose.”

“Can you hold the wheel?” Ada asked.

He held it while she unwound the string. It came away in a fuzzy, stubborn knot. Ada checked the axle for more strands, then slid the washer and wheel back into place. She turned the nut until it was snug, leaving the wheel room to spin.

This time, the wheel turned smoothly. Ada pushed the empty cart across the paving stones. No rattle, no scrape—just the soft bump of its wheels over the cracks.

Niko lifted one end of the plant tray. Ada took the other, and together they set it in the cart. They pushed toward the sunny wall, stopping once to shift a pot that leaned against its neighbor. The rain began to patter on the fig leaves as they reached the sheltered corner.

Ada returned the spanner to Mr. Rafi and tucked the green string into the little tin where lost bits of things were kept. Then she rolled the cart back beside the bench.

A bead of rain slid down the cart’s blue side and gathered beneath the quiet wheel. Inside the cart, six tomato leaves trembled in the breeze.
